Case report
Stiff-person like syndrome in a patient with
multiple pituitary hormone deﬁciencies
Chroni E, Papadimitriou A, Avramidis T, Terentiou AE, Tzioras C,
Divari R. Stiff-person like syndrome in a patient with multiple pituitary
hormone deﬁciencies.
Acta Neurol Scand 2000: 102: 403–405. # Munksgaard 2000.
A patient with long-standing, occult pituitary insufﬁciency, who
developed painful muscle stiffness and superimposed spasms, closely
resembling stiff-person syndrome, was described. Complete resolution of
neuromuscular symptoms with hormone replacement in this case, as well
as in a previously reported one, led to the suggestion that a syndrome like
stiff-person could represent a rare consequence of multiple pituitary
hormone deﬁciencies.
E. Chroni 1, A. Papadimitriou 1,
T. Avramidis 1, A. E. Terentiou 1,
C. Tzioras 2, R. Divari 1
From the Departments of 1Neurology and
2Endocrinology, Red Cross Hospital, Athens, Greece
Key words: stiff-person syndrome; pituitary hormone
deﬁciencies
E. Chroni, Department of Neurology, University Hospital
of Patras, P.O. Box 1045, Rion 26500
Tel./Fax: 01 03 061 993949
Accepted for publication July 5, 2000
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is an unusual neuro-
logical disorder characterized by progressive
rigidity of axial and limb muscles with super-
imposed painful, often stimulus induced, spasms.
Although SPS has often been associated with
various, mainly autoimmune, disorders (such as
diabetes mellitus type I) (1, 2), its treatment is
basically unrelated to any coexisting disease and
occasionally symptomatic (1, 3).
There was a single report of a case of pituitary
insufﬁciency and SPS, which was resolved with
hormone replacement (4). We present a similar case.
Case report
A 51-year-old woman was referred for investigation
of painful muscle stiffness in lower spine and both
legs. Sixteen months prior to admission, the patient
began to experience intermittent cramping pains
of thigh muscles, which gradually became more
frequent and ﬁnally permanent, involving also
abdominal and lower back muscles.
Her past history was unremarkable, until the age
of 30, when the normal delivery of her third child
was followed by severe postpartum haemorrhage.
From then menstruation, which was normal from
the age of 12, became very infrequent and ceased at
48 years of age. The patient reported that within the
next 2 years following the obstetric incident, she
presented intolerance to cold, eyebrow hair loss and
photosensitive, pruritic face rash.
Physical examination showed a well developed
female of normal intellect with dry, cold skin,
characteristic ‘‘waxy’’ or alabaster pale complexion
of the face and generalized eyebrow, axillary and
pubic hair loss. Her temperature was 36.5 uC, pulse
90 and blood pressure 110/65 mmHg. The thyroid
gland was not palpable. On motor examination,
there was normal muscle bulk and strength. Muscle
tone was markedly increased in the proximal parts of
the lower limbs (especially adductors and ﬂexors),
moderately increased in the abdominal and lower
paraspinal area and normal elsewhere. Passive
movements of hip or knee joints showed marked,
stable resistance throughout the entire range of
motion and triggered painful ﬂexor spasms.
Walking presented great difﬁculty, since in the
upright position her knees were permanently ﬂexed
to 90–100 degrees and hip up to 40–60 degrees. In the
supine position, the examiner’s arm could freely pass
under the tunnel formed between the patient’s waist

and bed mattress, due to ﬁxed lumbar hyperlordosis.

Tendon reﬂexes were brisk and symmetrical with
ﬂexor plantar responses. Cranial nerves, sensory and
cerebellar systems were intact. There were no signs
of arthritis. Close observation revealed that muscle
stiffness without, however, superimposed spasms,
persisted during sleep.
The ﬁndings of nerve conduction study in the
upper and lower limbs were normal. Needle
electromyography (EMG) of thigh, lower para-
spinal and abdominal muscles bilaterally revealed
continuous ﬁring of normal motor unit potentials,
which could not be suppressed volitionally. In
addition, brief bursts of synchronous motor unit
discharges were elicited in antagonist muscle pairs
by unexpected sound, tap or voluntary action.
EMG exam of muscles in the upper limbs, upper
trunk and distal parts of the lower limbs showed
normal silent period at rest. Fibrillations, fascicu-
lations, or myotonic discharges were not found in
any muscles. Study of cutaneo-muscular reﬂexes in
the legs using the technique described by Meinck
et al. (5), disclosed enhanced widespread responses
(especially from quadriceps bilaterally) with abnor-
mally low stimulus threshold.
Routine blood tests showed mild anaemia (Ht
31.1%–Hb 11 g/dlt), leukopenia (WBC 3.400/mm
3)
and hyperlipidemia type IIb. Blood glucose, serum
protein electrophoresis and CSF analysis were
normal. Organ and non-organ speciﬁc autoantibody
screening, including antibodies against glutamic
acid decarboxylase (GAD), pancreatic islet cell,
thyroid, adrenal, AchR and cell nuclei, was negative.
An abnormal routine thyroid function panel
(Table 1) in association with the presence of
characteristic alabaster face, the hair loss and the
history of postpartum haemorrhage demanded
further investigation of pituitary gland function.
Brain-CT scan disclosed extremely narrow sella
turcica with an atrophic and displaced pituitary
gland. Assessment of pituitary function revealed
that: 1) TSH level was inappropriately low for the
thyroxine value. 2) The basal value of cortisol was
low (free urine cortisol was 2.86 mg/24 h). 3) There
was insufﬁcient response of TSH, FSH/LH, ACTH
and GH to stimulation with TRH, LHRH, CRH
and GHRH respectively (Table 1). These results
suggested a multiple anterior pituitary hormone
deﬁciency.
Therapeutic trials with phenytoin, diazepam at a
dosage of 40 mg/day (further increase of the dose
was restricted by the patient’s intolerance) and
injections of botulin toxin type A at a total dose of
5600 units over 3 weeks time were only partially
beneﬁcial. Consequently, to replace the hormones,
the patient was started on hydrocortisone 30 mg/d
and thyroxine in gradually increasing doses up to
100 mg daily. With this substitution hormone
therapy, over the next 6 months, the patient’s
stiffness, pain and hypertonus completely disap-
peared, while her stance and gait became normal. A
repeat EMG showed almost normal voluntary
relaxation of all previously involved muscles.
Discussion
We have presented a patient with progressive, lower
trunk, proximal leg muscle stiffness and super-
imposed paroxysms of stimulus induced painful
spasms. This case bears close similarity to SPS,
including the characteristic lumbar lordosis (1, 6),
except that, unlike the classical syndrome, the
symptoms persisted during sleep and the upper
trunk musculature was spared. The EMG ﬁndings,
i.e. continuous activity of normal motor units and
exaggerated cutaneo-muscular reﬂexes, not seen in
other common causes of muscle tightness such as

dystonia or spasticity (7), advocated in favour of
SPS. Myotonia and neuromyotonia were excluded
by the EMG results. Encephalomyelitis of inﬂam-
matory or paraneoplastic nature and local lesions of
CNS, known to cause similar motor disturbances
(1, 3), were also excluded by the absence of signs of
brainstem or long tracks dysfunction and suppor-
tive laboratory results.
Incidental, dynamic endocrine testing in our
patient led to the diagnosis of multiple pituitary
deﬁciency, which preceded muscle stiffness by many
years and was probably due to postpartum pituitary
necrosis. A similar case with the clinical and
electrophysiologic picture of stiff-person syndrome
as part of a complex form of hypopituitarism has
been previously reported, and, as in our patient, it
responded to hormonal therapy (4). However,
unlike that case, our patient developed the neuro-
logical syndrome many years after the suspected
onset of endocrine insufﬁciency. The highly variable

degree of pituitary insufﬁciency in this context (8)
and the possible role of the menopause in the
endocrine dysfunction of our patient could account
for this discrepancy.
Complete cessation of muscle stiffness and
cramps in response to hormone replacement
therapy, while standard treatments for SPS had
failed, suggested that the neuromuscular symptoms
were closely related to the endocrine disturbance.
Cortisol was more likely to act through correction
of hormone deﬁciencies rather than as immuno-
suppressive since there were no evidences to
support an immune mediated process. Endocrine
disorders, in particular hypothyroidism, are known
to cause painful muscle cramps and stiffness
accompanied, however, by Hoffmann’s sign and
EMG changes not found in our case, i.e.
spontaneous activity at rest or electrically silent
myoedema (9).
We suggested that a syndrome like stiff-person
could represent a rare consequence of multiple
pituitary hormone deﬁciencies, requiring no spe-
ciﬁc treatment. Cases such as the present one allow
speculation for the possible role of hormones
(especially ACTH-cortisol) in the motor sub-
systems balance.
